channel.title: CuriousMarc
channel.description: Videos documenting restorations of exceptional vintage electronics and early computers, space hardware and the odd mechanical calculator or Teletype. It often showcases my Hewlett-Packard test equipment collection and, from time to time, my R2-D2 robot build. Things rarely work when I start, but almost always do when I end. A nerdy place for your inner engineer, to celebrate engineering exploits o

videos.t: Senna Drive with #25 Chain
videos.desc: For illustrating my build log on Astromech.net. This is my Senna drive. I changed my link chain from the recommended #35 to a finer #25 chain. Someone commented on my blog that they solved the sticky chain problem by using gears with just one more tooth (and keeping the #35 chain). Now I can see what the problem really is: chain too coarse for wrapping around almost 180 deg. on a sprocket with too few teeth. Making the chain finer and having more teeth in the gears will solve the problem. I did both...

videos.t: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer Repair pt. 2
videos.desc:
Closer look at the YTO error while exercising the 3 possible YTO tuning modes. 

I donwloaded the repair manuals from Artek Media (great service by the way). I learned that for spans greater than 20 MHz, the YTO oscillator is tuned using the main coil. For spans between 1 MHz and 20 MHz, the smaller FM driving coil is used. And below 1 MHz, the YTO is not swept at all, sweeping is from the 50 MHz oscillator. I was curious to see if the error was different depending on the span. It is. Smoking gun here. My first target would be the coil drivers in board A22.

videos.t: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer Repair YTO unlock pt. 1
videos.desc:
Taking a break from R2 building, and attempting to repair my HP 8568B with YTO unlock error. I have only seen one documented repair blog on this (on an 8566B), but apparently it is a common problem, so maybe this will be helpful to others.

I recently bought a vintage HP 8568B 100Hz-1.5GHz Spectrum Analyzer to add to my collection. Why this particular one? Because I consider it a masterpiece of awesomely engineered measurement equipment, that is in some ways still unsurpassed. The McIntosh of spectrum analyzers. And you can have it now for pennies on the dollar. 

My local surplus store had 3

videos.t: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer Repair pt. 4
videos.desc: Continuing the debug of my HP8568B with the YTO unlock error. Looking at the phase lock loop signal output from A6.

videos.t: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer Repair pt. 5 and success!
videos.desc: My HP8568B with YTO unlock error is fixed! Of all things, from a tip from Mark Palmer who watched my previous videos. He told me to adjust R39, and I soon as I touched it, the error disappeared. The pot wiper must not have been making proper contact. That pot controls the DC bias to the FM YTO coil. Well, happy ending thanks to YouTube. Many thanks Mark.

videos.t: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer Repair pt. 3
videos.desc: Continuing my debug of my HP8568 with the YTO unlock error. Looking at the YTO FM coil signal on board A22.

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 1
videos.desc:
My HP 8662A synthesized signal generator has gone bonkers. It has error code 99, subcode 04. The signal is 5 MHz off, with a horribly noisy spectrum. Yet another daunting debug problem - as someone put it mildly, this is not an oscillator for beginners. 

See part 2: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BXfo08jDuLI

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 3
videos.desc:
From the previous video, I know the error is dependent on the x.x MHz digits, which the part of the frequency that's synthetized by the low frequency N-loop. But that loop checks out fine. It's the loop that adds this with the lower frequency digits that seems to be failing. But it shouldn't have any periodicity with the N-loop, unless there is some weird circuitry. Turns out, there actually is! 
See part 4: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ds-nSPl0Rdc

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 2
videos.desc:
After reading up on the principle of operation, I get a detail look at the error. It depends on only two digits (the x.x MHz) digits, and is independent of the value of the higher or lower digits. This gives me an idea of where to look for a fault.
See part 3: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3j3x_ObZ2gE

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 4
videos.desc:
Getting closer to the fault. Checking the pre-tune circuitry, since it's the simplest measurement to start with. 

See part 5: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9ZyRken6N4w

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 8 and success!
videos.desc:
I got it all fixed! I finally got my VCO adjusted within range. The trick was to find and temporarily remove two soldered jumper wires on the VCO board before re-doing the adjustment procedure shown in video 6 (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=150dNw8Ygq0) . Now it works like a champ.s
One more fine piece of equipment repaired.

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 7
videos.desc:
In the previous video, we could not adjust the Sum Loop VCO card back in spec. Let's pull it out and see if we can find something wrong with it.s
See happy ending in part 8: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dUFHAx3IwJ0

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 6
videos.desc:
In the previous video, we found that the VCO is tuning was too low through the range. But there is an adjustment just for that, so if I can adjust it back I should be home free. Unfortunately, I do not seem to have enough adjustment to bring it back in range. 

See part 7: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H3w69DEN9EA

videos.t: HP 8662A synthesized signal generator repair part 5
videos.desc:
Checking if the VCO follows the pre-tuning which we checked in the previous video. It follows, but it is way off. Maybe it is out of adjustment.
See part 6: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=150dNw8Ygq0

videos.t: Using the HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer with the HP 8444A Opt. 059 Tracking Generator
videos.desc:
[Edit: I got even better performance out of it, check my update here:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qoMJXwRv-v4]

I was curious how an HP8444A tracking generator option 59 would work with a HP8568B spectrum analyzer. Answer is: much better than anticipated. These units were not really designed to work together, as you can tell from the cabinet design that doesn't even match at all (but the design is an exact match for the older 8554B spectrum analyzer). They are a generation or two apart, one is a relatively simple all analog tracker, the other a very sophisticated, reference locked, compute

videos.t: Update: HP 8568B Spectrum Analyzer with the HP 8444A Tracking Generator
videos.desc:
This is an addition to my previous video: https://www.youtube.com/edit?video_id=_yZOW_aABlk
After finishing all adjustments, this old analog HP8444A generator is even better than I thought. Flatness well within +/- 1 dB over the whole 100 kHz to 1.5 GHz range. Very well engineered analog unit, and still working great today. Laboratory quality HP equipment might have lost most of its value, but none of its performance (that is, after you repair it...).

Except for the date mechanism which I still need to take completely apart. The motor is hooked up to a master pulse generator, and the minutes, hours and day of the week now work perfectly. videos.t: Solari Udine Dator 10 Flip Clock Restoration Part 1
videos.desc:
My vintage Solari Udine Dator 10, 1950's industrial clock from Italy, just came in! It's the most famous of flip clocks: Solari is the company that invented the flip panels you used to see at airports. From an Italian seller on e-bay, it was a long and risky adventure to buy it and actually get it shipped here. It took the guy 3 month with a lot of convincing. At one point e-bay arbitration even canceled the transaction. But somehow perseverance paid of, and the clock is in good shape and eminently repairable, and a slave clock as I had correctly inferred. 
By the way, what I say in the video

videos.t: Vintage HP 7225 Plotter and HP 82901 5.25" floppy demo with HP 85
videos.desc:
I got on a tangent restoring HP 85's to use as lab equipment controllers. These machines are such a classic milestone in micro-computer design. It's the scientific "Macintosh" of the pre-PC area. 
Could not resist to acquire a plotter for it, which I was able to restore. I love the older gantry-style ones, which are so much more fun to watch than the later cheaper ones that move the paper. Here is a demo.

videos.t: HP 85 demo: GPIB lab equipment control made simple!
videos.desc:
My recently repaired vintage Tek scope, HP 8568B spectrum analyzer and HP 8663A frequency synthesizer all feature HP-IB control (today known as IEEE 488 or GPIB bus). They needed a nice controller. But controlling them from a modern computer would be absolutely no fun. Doing it from a proper vintage 1970's HP 85A computer, though, is a load of fun. That's what this little amazing computer was made for. It speaks HP-IB natively, is a cinch to program, and looks cute and period correct.

Here is a short demo.

That sent me into a loop of restoring HP-85's, whose printer belts are failing and tap

videos.t: Building Lab Power Supplies out of Vaultz cases and old ATX supplies
videos.desc:
Good high-amperage 12V power supply are always handy for amateur robotics work. I built 3 of them yesterday. Two "vintage looking" ones with analog current displays using a cheap 12V standard "brick" supply and a Vaultz media or CD case. A third one by recycling an old ATX computer power supply - less pretty but more efficient. And it gives you all sorts of voltages. Complete uncut footage with dummy load test and release of magic smoke...
For Vaultz case ones I invented my own construction method, I got a cheap 12V supply brick from there:
http://www.robotmarketplace.com/products/0-PS-100W-12

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 11: HP 85 demo playing slot and maze games
videos.desc:
Final part 11 of our HP 85A restoration. It's all back together, all the way back from the dead, with printer and tape that works, and it can even read DC2000 QIC tapes. Let's play!
You can see the DC2000 tape just barely fits in there. But it slides in without forcing. I'd rather leave the mechanism as original as possible and just carefully wiggle it in there, not a big deal.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 10. fixing with the tape stall error
videos.desc: Part 10 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Sure enough, I put it back together but the tape stalled. Then disaster struck. I hit a seemingly interminable series of deeper and deeper setbacks trying to chase the stall problem, all the way to killing the machine. Unfortunately not recorded as I was too panicked to take videos. That included faulty connectors everywhere, several complete disassemlies of the Pittman motor for naught, and finally the big one, an accidental spark that killed the machine for good (power off the machine before you work on it!). Completely dead. Would not show any sign

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 9. Tape PCB modification, putting the drive back together.
videos.desc: Part 9 of our HP 85A restoration effort. To reliabaly use the DC200 / QIC tapes, or the newly made Athana DC100A original format tape, you have to add a resistor on the board. This is because the magnetic tape material is slightly more coercive, which is probably why they are more reliable too. This modification is non-destructive, it will not prevent you from using original vintage tapes, if you ever find any that still work that is.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 8. Tape drive capstan wheel modification and re-coat.
videos.desc: Part 8 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Capstan modification and re-coat. I make a new taller capstan so that the drive can accept the DC2000 / QIC 40 tape cartridges. It's quite involved, I have to bring in the big tools. If you don't want to bother, just recoat the original capstan in heat-shrink tubing and let it wrap on top, there is just enough height for the capstan to catch the bottom of the DC2000 drive wheel. That's what I have on my other machine and it works fine for now.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 7. Brief explanation of the QIC tape modification.
videos.desc: Part 7 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Now I am going to make it noticeably more complicated. Not only do I want to re-coat the capstan of the tape drive, but I want to adapt the drive to the QIC 40/80 (DC 2000) tape format. The original HP tapes, the DC100A, did not make it to this day. They were already noticeably unreliable in their time, and none that I know of made it alive today. I tried 3 different sources, including unopened "new" ones, "reconditioned" ones, my own repaired ones, and none worked. The magnetic material is just gone. There is one maker (Athana) that still makes new one

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 6. Taking the tape mechanism apart.
videos.desc: Part 3 of our HP 85A restoration effort. I need to take the tape mechanism apart to fix the "gooey capstan" syndrome. Mine was so gooey that the rubber completey flowed away in the mechanism. There was nothing left on the capstan wheel itself except color. Beware of the thin wires for the motor speed encoder lamp, which have to be pulled out gently from the PCB.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 5. Comparison of my two machines, hidden signatures.
videos.desc: Part 5 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Taking a breather after the printer repairs. Since I had the two machines out for the printer head exchange, I took a family movie. If you thought the Apple MacIntosh were the first people to sign the inside of their cases, think again, and see where the tradition actually comes from. One of the machines even has a a flower or butterfly drawn in that was waiting all these years to be re-discovered!

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 4. Putting new belts in, print head adjustment routine.
videos.desc:
Part 4 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Putting the new belts in is very easy. Adjusting the print head position correctly is less obvious, although not difficult either. There is a specific procedure to follow. You need to uncouple the head from the motor, put the motor and head in a specific position, then re-couple them.
The two belts can be ordered online:
https://sdp-si.com/eStore/Catalog/PartNumber/A%206B16-175012

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 3. Changing the print head.
videos.desc: Part 3 of our HP 85A restoration effort. I wanted to exchange the print heads of the two machines to put all the best parts on one machine. It is not as easy as just changing the belts, but hopefully you won't need it if you print head is fine. But in case you need it, here is a video tutorial on that arcane subject.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 2. Removing the printer belts.
videos.desc: Part 2 of our HP 85A restoration effort. Repairing the printer should actually be quite easy. Here is how to procure new belts and how to remove the old ones. Mine were in terrible shape.

videos.t: HP 85 Repair Part 1 - Opening the case
videos.desc: The Hewlett Packard HP 85A is one of the best pre-PC personal scientific computer. Actually it is really a very high end programmable calculator with graphics, I/O and storage. One of the many touches that makes them so special is the integrated graphics screen, printer and tape storage. However, tape and printer usually don't work anymore, you'll see why in this video. My two units were no exception. So lets try to repair it. This particular tape unit is a 1260S, the S meaning that a SCSI interface was retrofitted to the native Pertec unit. I was going to hook it up to a modern PC, but why not try the Mac SE? This is one of the few personal computers that talked SCSI-1 natively. After finding the right DB-25 to SCSI Centronics cable, I was able to connect the two.

videos.desc:
Here is my new old IBM 29 Keypunch. The grand-son of the IBM 26 which I also have. It's now in the lab, all cleaned up and looking pretty new. But looks can be deceiving. Unlike the older looking IBM 26 which I also show in this video, the 29 doesn't work at all yet. Does not even power up. This punch came from an audacious rescue operation that Carl Claunch recently mounted in Kansas. He brought a whole truckload of vintage IBM equipment including an awesome IBM 1130.

videos.t: IBM 029 Keyunch Restoration 2: First signs of life
videos.desc:
The IBM 029 is slowly emerging from its 30 years coma. I was able to force card feed cycles manually by pushing down on the clutch relay. That must have loosened up a few things, as it then started to respond to feed cards and register commands from the keyboard all of a sudden. It won't punch nor release the card, and doesn't even know it has a card loaded apparently - keeps registering and feeding as if the station were empty. But that's its first encouraging signs of life! Needs to re-learn how to walk I guess...

videos.desc: After painful work tracing, cleaning and readjusting one defective cams after another with nothing much to show for it, I finally traced a malfunctioning switch, hidden under the escape solenoid. And finally, after I repaired that, everything started to fall into place. The card registered correctly. Punching came back to life. Incredibly, all the punches work, no mechanical adjustment needed. And so does the read station, it duplicates fine. I got printing to start working a little bit later. [Edit 12/26/2017:] Ken Shirriff has finally explained the reason for the insane keyboard arrangement, you can read his post here http://www.righto.com/2017/12/repairing-1960s-era-ibm-keypunch.html . videos.t: IBM 029 Keypunch Restoration 7 - Print Head
videos.desc: The print head, with a mechanism design that dates back to the 1940's, is a marvel of engineering. Entirely mechanical yet very small and fast, it is probably the first dot matrix printer ever made. It relies on a very original arrangement, using very fine, long wires pushed by a code plate which moves by minute amounts. At the code plate end, wires are widely separated, then they run through a long tube, and at the print end they are very close together. Oh-so-clever. Restoring the print head was tricky precision business, but gave me a chance to look at this incredible mechanism. And then I

videos.t: Documation Punched Card Reader Restoration Part 1 - Blower and Mechanical Work
videos.desc: First step in the restoration of the 1970's Documation M600 Punched Card Reader. It didn't do too well on first power up as you can see in the first video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8V9EOjD9kuE ... But I finally get the blower, mechanics and power supply issues straightened out, up to a point where it reads ONE card. That's better than zero. I'll call that progress! videos.t: Documation Punched Card Reader Part 3 - Found a bad chip?
videos.desc:
Continuing to restore my 1970's vintage punched card reader. Forget what I said in Part 2, the fault seems to be a little further away in one of the counters. Here is how I found it with the vintage HP 1670 Logic Analyzer. So I think at least one bad chip. I have ordered a replacement, to be continued.

See next: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0YAFc1G5NxY

videos.t: Documation Punched Card Reader Part 4 - It works again!
videos.desc: The bad counter chip identified in part 3 was the indeed the culprit. I changed it and now it doesn't get stuck after reading just one card. One more modification for the right-hand cut corner (a known issue that my friends alerted had told me about) and it reads a whole deck at speed! I think it's resurrected.

videos.t: Documation Punched Card Reader Part 5 - Final Output Test
videos.desc: This is the last test for the 1970's Documation M600 Punched Card Reader. I am looking at the data output from a purpose-made test card. At first it was not reading row 12 correctly. I suspected that was from my attempted modification to read cards with right-hand corner cuts. A hidden trace below an IC had escaped me (thanks Carl for pointing it out!). I modified the modification, and now it reads cards properly and can read right hand cut cards. I declare it fully restored (and improved)! Next step will be to make a modern computer interface.

The HP 2225 ThinkJet printer was a technology tour de force in its time. Cheaper and smaller than other competing personal printers (maybe save for the thermal ones), it was the first practical consumer inkjet printer. I found this one laying on its back, in pretty sad shape, at a surplus store. It is one of the rarer and original "A" models with the HP-IB interface. Made in 1985, it looks and feels like a much more modern machine. It

videos.t: Vintage HP 21MX computer arrives for restoration
videos.desc: The 21MX is an early HP mini-computer introduced in 1974. It is the first in what would later evolve into the rather long-lived family of HP-1000 computers (HP-1000 M, E and F). It was a technological first, the first mini-computer relying on semiconductor memory (CMOS chips from then new startup Intel), instead of the magnetic core memory used in 1950-1960's computers. Logic is made of individual TTL circuit gates and some CuTL (the first integrated circuit series that was used in the Apollo Moon mission computer), carried over from the HP 2100 it replaced. And yes, it has blinkenlights on th

videos.t: 5.25" Floppy Part 1: Drive Installation
videos.desc:
Guide on how to intall a 5.25" floppy drive. I needed to read and recreate old 5.25" floppies for my pre-PC era computers and HP instruments, so I got a few old floppy drives. I thought hooking them up was going to be a piece of cake. It wasn't. I got my fair share of "Floppy Disk Fail (40)" and "Disk Not Ready" errors before I could make sense of it. Before I forget what I did to eventually make it work, here is a video to help sort out the many 5.25" drive types, drive jumpers, cables and (old) BIOS settings. 
Part 2 shows how to work at sector level to read anything including non-PC formats

videos.t: 5.25" Floppy Part 2: (very) low level DOS Floppy utilities tutorial
videos.desc:
How to use low level tools to read a floppy diskette. Now that my vintage 5.25" floppy drive is installed correctly (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rbxPW86B84E), I can read vintage 5.25" PC floppies. Under DOS, low level tools allow to inspect partially damaged discs that Windows or DOS can't read, or discs that are not formatted for the PC and can otherwise not be read at all. Omnidisk and DiskImage are two such tools. I try it on a partially damaged HP LIF diskette. 

Omnidisk available from: http://www.shlock.co.uk/Utils/OmniDisk/OmniDisk.htm#Downloads
ImageDisk available from: http://www.

videos.t: 5 25" Floppy Part 3: Recreating a HP LIF (not PC compatible) Vintage Diskette
videos.desc: How to recreate an odd format vintage floppy. After part 1 (https://youtu.be/rbxPW86B84E) and part 2 (https://youtu.be/ANym0BgT_IE), we finally get to what I am most interested in: re-creating old non-PC diskettes from raw binary images. The binary images like the ones used in emulators or hex dumps don't have sector and format information. You need to add it before you can recreate an old diskette that can be run in a real machine. In this example, I am trying to re-create a game diskette for my venerable HP-85. The HP-85 uses a non-PC format with the following attributes: 35 tracks, 16 secto

videos.t: Debugging the 1959 IBM 1401 Computer at the Computer History Museum
videos.desc:
A little behind the scenes look at what it takes to keep the two giant IBM 1401 "Compusaurs" running at the computer history museum. Today the tape drives decided not to work. 

The IBM 1401, introduced in 1959, is one of the first transistorized computers, and certainly the most successful computer of the early 1960's: by 1965, half of the world's computers were 1401's. Only two are known to be still functioning - and here they are.

Compared to my humble restorations, this is major hardware and it could not be done by one person alone - it takes a full team of very dedicated people to keep i

videos.t: HP and Overland 9-Track Tape Drives Demo
videos.desc:
Three out of four of my vintage 9-track tape drives are working of tonight, including for the very first time my venerable HP 7970E. Time for a video! Each of them is special. The jewel of the collection is the HP 7970E, a tape drive introduced in 1970. I believe this E model is from 1974 or thereabouts. It is serious hardware, and weighs in at 140 lbs. I needed to resurrect it for my HP 21MX system of the same period. It talks only to HP equipment using HP-IB, so it is quite a challenge to bring online. The other tapes were acquired mostly to support this one. 

The HP 88780B is its grandson,

videos.t: Qualstar 1260S 9-Track Magnetic Tape Drive Repair
videos.desc:
This shows how I adjusted my 1990 vintage Qualstar 9-track tape drive to bring it back to life. 
Another arcane video mostly to help other owners of Qualstar tapes to adjust theirs.

My Qualstar 1260S failed to read any tape and was squeaking when repositioning the tape. Cleaning the tape path got read of the squealing and got it to read something. But I still had many retries during read and writes. I proceeded to readjust the write current and read gain to get rid of errors. While checking the read gain, I discovered one head had way too low a signal, which which was traced to a bad head con

videos.t: Vintage Daisy Wheel Printer on WinXP - or the hard way to make a typewriter
videos.desc: Can you still hook up a clunky vintage daisy wheel printer to a modern Windows computer? Of course you can! And even make a typewriter out of it. I had  first shown this early 1980's vintage Juki daisy wheel printer in another video (see here: https://youtu.be/6gjln8KygG0), where I hooked it up to a pre-PC computer of the same era. A viewer asked if it would be possible to connect it to a modern computer and OS. Someone immediately answered no. I didn't think this was correct, so I wanted to try it out for myself...

videos.t: HP 59401A Bus Analyzer and HP 10342B Bus Preprocessor for HP-IB Bus Sniffing
videos.desc: HP-IB was a high-performance bus for connecting peripherals and test instruments, introduced by HP in the late 1960’s. Today it’s known and standardized as GPIB (also called IEEE 488), and still popular in test instruments. At the time, this HP-only novelty vastly outperformed competition. Of course, HP also made great test instruments for debugging their bus: the charming, easy to use, paddle-driven HP 59401A, introduced in 1977, and the later and less charming but more efficient HP 19342B preprocessor for its 16xx logic analyzer series, which I both demonstrate while debugging the HP 7970E 9

videos.t: Facit TK Mechanical Calculator Demo (1936)
videos.desc:
This is a demo of the Facit TK mechanical calculator. This Swedish pinwheel calculator was introduced in 1936 and got famous for introducing number entry with a numerical keypad instead of levers. Despite its simplicity, it has numerous clever features, a few demonstrated here. A legacy of the Facit calculator to this day is the digital numerical keypad with the zero at the bottom.

See companion video of the mechanism inside here:
http://youtu.be/5utHg7tG10c

videos.t: Inside the Facit TK Mechanical Calculator
videos.desc:
Companion video to my Facit Calculator demo, see here:
https://youtu.be/cRGu1OBFPrc
Trying to show what goes on inside this clever calculator designed in 1936.
For a more detailed description of the mechanism, head to John Wolf’s excellent mechanical calculator site here:
http://www.johnwolff.id.au/calculators/Tech/FacitC1-13/C113.htm

videos.t: Real laser hologram
videos.desc: Here is a hologram I made about 30 years ago. Not the fake computer generated YouTube kind or the rainbow thing on your credit card. The real analog thing, made with a laser and holographic plate. I had not looked at it in probably as many years, as you actually need a fairly good laser source to see it. But today I found a real nice laser at my local surplus store (WeirdStuff, they sell on ebay too)! I had to have it. As soon as I came home I rigged up this hologram projection setup. Here it is in all it's analog beauty and full laser 3D!

videos.t: HP-85 Vintage Computer CRT Monitor Repair
videos.desc: My beloved 1979 HP-85 started failing! Arcane debug session into CRT horizontal scan circuitry follows. Hopefully it may help others to revive their HP-85's with the same problem. Fortunately the schematics are available, so can I find what's wrong and repair it (video is 8 minutes but it took me two evenings...). So I can play FatCat again. Yay.

videos.t: HP-85 vintage computer: repairing the tape capstan with an O-ring
videos.desc:
Here is another video about repairing the HP-85 tape drive. The Hewlett Packard 85 is a pre-PC era scientific personal computer. The original capstan wheel coating invariably turns to goop on this all important peripheral. I already have a series of videos on how to repair and modify the tape drive for the better QIC tapes:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0lSHzM2pabw
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B0TPuLBEgR0
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7IQKCiS0w2s
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gkgMEXyavOg
But I have long term reliability issues with the previous capstan re-coating methods. Here is an a

videos.t: HP 85 computer draws anime on a vintage HP pen plotter
videos.desc: Always fascinating to see a pen plotter draw. The pre-PC era HP 85 "computer" is from 1979 and the HP 7225 plotter is from 1978. Not bad for ancient computer fossils! Restoration details shown in my other videos. OK, OK, enough comments about the music! I give up! The song is Ievan Polka and is in Finnish. Here is the original YouTube link: https://youtu.be/4om1rQKPijI . 22 Million views and counting. Here is Hatsune Miku's version: https://youtu.be/qmf9JkedPR8 . 33 Million views and counting. It's is an anime reference, see Leekspin here: https://youtu.be/1wnE4vF9CQ4. 9 Million views and coun

videos.t: HP 2631G Dot Matrix Printer Restoration (vintage 1978)
videos.desc:
I found a HP 2631G printer at a local recycler, under a dusty pile of other unremarkable worthless parallel port printers. This is no ordinary vintage printer though.  A heavy dot matrix beast from 1978, 15" paper, 180 characters per second, HP-IB interface. I had great hopes and procured a new ribbon (you can still find them!). Sadly when I turned it on it was motionless. I set to work to return it back to its former glory.

See the full demo after the repair:
https://youtu.be/YS9dGYUbNd0

videos.t: Bye Bye Babbage: the most awesome mechanical calculator good bye party
videos.desc:
There are amazing mechanical calculators, and then there is the Babbage Difference Engine #2. On loan to the Computer History Museum for the last 8 years, it is going back to our benefactor and rightful owner Nathan Myhrvold next week. This is the most amazing mechanical calculator I have ever seen - and by some margin. It was quite a noisy party when I recorded, so I recommend to turn on the closed captions to follow along.

It is the achievement of a lone 19th century British genius, the result of a lifetime of theoretical designs with pen and paper only.  Designed by mathematician Charles B

videos.t: ASCII art demo with vintage HP 85 computer, HP 7970E 9-track tape and HP 2631G dot matrix printer
videos.desc:
What do you with a 1970's vintage  Hewlett-Packard computer, 9-track magnetic tape and dot matrix printer? Print ASCII art of course!

This is an unlikely assortment of a HP 85 scientific computer (1979), a HP 7970 magnetic reel-to-reel tape drive (1970) and a HP 2631 professional dot-matrix printer (1977). Although they all communicate via HP-IB, this is before a standard was established, and the higher end peripherals were not meant at all to connect to the diminutive HP 85 personal computer. In particular, the HP 7970 tape needs a bit of hardware help to talk to the HP 85. I had to make a m

videos.t: Ferrari and Alfa Romeo gathering at the Blackhawk museum
videos.desc: There was an informal gathering of the Ferrari club and Alfa Romeo club at the Blackhawk museum last month, on the occasion of Enzo Ferrari's birthday. Here are a few of my favorite cars outside and inside the museum. And the small cute white Alfa Romeo is a Giulietta Sprint 1300.

videos.t: IBM Selectric II Typewriter Golf Ball Madness!
videos.desc:
My 1973 all-mechanical Selectric II "golf ball" typewriter has just been repaired. Let's try my collection of balls! OK, I have quite a few... You'll be surprised by the quality of the result. Oldie but goodie as they say.You can see the inside and short repair video here: https://youtu.be/lBrt2LlH6Rk , and an explanation of how the amazing mechanism works here: https://youtu.be/bRCNenhcvpw 

Special thanks to Stan P. for the donation of this machine!

videos.t: IBM Selectric II typewriter repairs
videos.desc:
This IBM Selectric II needs a little TLC. Sticky tab key (easy fix), out of alignment typeball (medium hard), and sticky/hesitant carriage return (totally unobvious). Great opportunity to look inside this insanely complicated, entirely mechanical, golf-ball typewriter from 1973.

Selectric documentation on my website here: https://www.curiousmarc.com/mechanical/ibm-selectric

videos.t: Debugging the 1959 IBM 729 Vacuum Column Tape Drive at the Computer History Museum
videos.desc:
Our magnificent IBM 729 7-track magnetic tape drive is giving us read and write errors. We attempt another heroic repair. Which is a great excuse to take a close look at its amazing innards. Looks like nothing in the video, but just putting the 3 brush blocks back was a 3 hour operation with mostly 6 hands at a time inside the drives - including mine, which is why there is no video documenting it. Hence the clapping at the end, we were quite relieved we did put it back together correctly!

Tape capacity is around 20 MB at the highest (800 cpi) density setting. Actually quite respectable if you

videos.t: Seminal Xerox Alto arrives for restoration
videos.desc:
Today is a big day. An original Xerox Alto, belonging to the Y-combinator, a startup incubator in the valley, came in for restoration. This machine is as rare at it is seminal, and is a gift of Alan Kay, of Xerox and Atari fame. 16 bit machine, not 32 as I say in the video.

Invented in nearby Xerox Parc (Palo Alto Research Center), it was so far ahead of it's time, it's hard to comprehend. It had the first GUI, complete with a mouse, and the first ever Ethernet interface - Ethernet was invented for this machine. On a 1973 mostly TTL design with originally 128k of memory. 

The Alto was only u

videos.t: HP Photosmart 3210 Inkjet Printer Head Repair and Cleaning
videos.desc:
After I repaired it, one of my cartridges went empty. I got the dreaded, non-resettable, "ink system has failed error 0xc18a0206", which is misleading printer techno-babble for: your cartridge is empty sooner than I expected. Not shown in the video, see instructions below on how to clear this. 

To clear the infamous "ink system has failed 0xc18a0206" error message (provided you unclogged the heads beforehand as in the video): hold cancel and OK while you power down, and keep holding while you power back up until it eventually powers down again. Then press power on, you'll enter the OOB NVRAM

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 1 - power supply restoration, disk drive surprise
videos.desc:
We begin our very gentle and progressive power up of the seminal Xerox Alto. No magic smoke, but one power supply is faulty. Opening it up reveals that it had a tough life, having suffered a catastrophic short of some sort, hastily repaired, and some traces almost entirely corroded through. But the source of the malfunction seems to be a somewhat classic case of bad electrolytic capacitors, way too far gone for any hope of reforming. After replacing them and repairing the supply, we turn our attention to the Diablo disc drive and cartridge, and have a bit of a surprise.
 
Many thanks to my CHM

videos.t: Divide by Zero on the Friden STW10 Mechanical Calculator
videos.desc:
Please, try a divide by zero! Pleeeeeease! What would happen? What if Katherine Johnson did that  in the movie Hidden Figures (this is the Friden that sits on her desk)? Would it catch fire? Would the rocket trajectory go to infinity? Now you are finally going to find out. Stick to the end for a little extra, a scene from another great movie that stars the Friden. This is a Friden STW 10 from 1956. 

Friden Calculator Playlist: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5_GbzkFwdKpuyPo8Ty83h8b

More about the Friden STW10 on my website:
https://www.curiousmarc.com/mechanical/friden-stw-10-me

videos.t: IBM Model 214 "Executary" Dictaphone (1961)
videos.desc: This beautiful IBM unit was given to me by my father when I was a child. He would bring back electronic things from work that didn't work. Already as a kid I was passionate about taking things apart and trying to repair them. I failed at this one, but I found it again in the attic when I last visited my parents, and I brought it back. It's even more beautiful than I remembered! It was introduced in 1961, and is creatively named an IBM Executary 214 (from "Executive Secretary" maybe?). It records on a 4" band instead of a tape, which makes the various recordings instantly accessible without any

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 2 - monitor restoration
videos.desc:
Our motley crew assembles again to fire up the monitor, which reluctantly comes back to life. A dead cap, a gooped up brightness pot and self induced mistakes stood in our way, but I suspect it was mainly the lazy CRT tube that needed much warm up before offering a feeble picture that got us confounded for a while. 

Huge thanks to Seattle's Living Computer Museum Keith Hayes for lending us their monitor test board.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 3 - disk drive bring up
videos.desc: We got our missing disc interface card, gift from Al Kossow (from his personal collection, not from the Computer History Museum!), so we can turn our attention to bringing up the disc. Carl Claunch is our leader for this phase, as he has restored many of these drives for his IBM 1130 (Diablos are IBM clones really). We are joined by Tim Curley representing the official PARC (the former Xerox Parc), who brings us a nice welcome gift. At the end of the day we got it to load the heads on the disc without damage, and display the famous "Ready" indicator. We  feel giddy and attempt a full up test.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 4 - first signs of processor life
videos.desc:
Last time we got the basic peripherals to work, but the machine seemed dead when we tried to boot. We now have to start the painstaking task of looking at the processor logic. Here we look for basic signs of processor activity: clocks and microtask switching. Ken Shirriff who researched the microcode and schematics led this session.

The Alto has a very peculiar architecture, where the processor runs every peripheral in microcode. For this, it continually switches between 16 micro-programmed tasks. Even the memory refresh is a processor driven microtask. And so is the display refresh, disk rea

videos.t: VCF West XI (2016): vintage computing festival highlights
videos.desc: There was much happening at the Vintage Computer Festival (VCF West) held at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, CA on Aug. 6-7, 2016. Many more exhibits and talks that fit in one video, or that I could possibly document while I was exhibiting at the same time. So this is just a sliver of it, made of my personal favorites. By chance I caught some of the award winners, including me!

videos.t: R2-D2 Build Day Aug  13 2016
videos.desc: Our informal San Francisco R2-D2 Builders Group gathering, for a build day, on Aug. 13, 2016. This video is dedicated to Kenny Baker, the dwarf actor who animated R2 from the inside, who passed away on this very date.

videos.t: Data IO 29B PROM Programmer Repair Part 1
videos.desc:
Vintage computers (and Arcade Games), particularly the micro-programmed ones like the Xerox Alto we are currently restoring, use old but very fast bipolar PROMs to hold the microcode. 
I need an old instrument to read them and to program them. Enter the Data I/O 29B with Unipak 2, fresh from ePay. It was the high-end EPROM and CPLD programmer of the time. Will it work (hint: usually eBay things don't).

videos.t: Data IO 29B PROM Programmer Repair Part 2
videos.desc:
Follow up to part 1 here: https://youtu.be/iYxf1etUIR0
I have a "repair rqd 71" error. My Unipak 2 is toast. Let's repair it!

Vintage computers (and Arcade Games), particularly the micro-programmed ones like the Xerox Alto we are currently restoring, use old but very fast bipolar PROMs to hold the microcode. 
I need an old instrument to read them and to program them. Enter the Data I/O 29B with Unipak 2, fresh from ePay. It was the high-end EPROM and CPLD programmer of the time.

videos.t: Data IO 29B PROM Programmer Demo: burning the HP 85 service ROM
videos.desc:
Finally, it's restored! This beautiful piece of vintage professional hardware is quite a popular device among retro computing and arcade gaming people, because it's so nice and it can program stuff all the way back to bipolar PROMs. But it's not that obvious how to set it up at first. So for public good, here this demo where I will show how to set up this old beast, and I use it to program the elusive Service ROM chip for my HP-85.

My many restoration videos on the DataIO 29B here:
Part 1: https://youtu.be/iYxf1etUIR0
Part 2 https://youtu.be/-sXAZ2LK2ws
Part 3 https://youtu.be/2CFvSM87GAM

videos.desc:
Follow up to part 3 here: https://youtu.be/2CFvSM87GAM
Now it can read but still can't program an EPROM! The @##$$%!! ebay machine is not cooperating. I promise we'll track down the last issue this time.

Vintage computers (and Arcade Games), particularly the micro-programmed ones like the Xerox Alto we are currently restoring, use old but very fast bipolar PROMs to hold the microcode. 
I need an old instrument to read them and to program them. Enter the Data I/O 29B with Unipak 2, fresh from ePay. It was the high-end EPROM and CPLD programmer of the time.

videos.desc:
Follow up to part 2 here: https://youtu.be/-sXAZ2LK2ws
I discovered a bad transistor in my Unipak 2. Can I find a replacement and fix it?

Vintage computers (and Arcade Games), particularly the micro-programmed ones like the Xerox Alto we are currently restoring, use old but very fast bipolar PROMs to hold the microcode. 
I need an old instrument to read them and to program them. Enter the Data I/O 29B with Unipak 2, fresh from ePay. It was the high-end EPROM and CPLD programmer of the time.

videos.t: Tektronix 577 Curve Tracer Repair and Demo
videos.desc: The Tektronix 577 is a superb vintage curve tracer. But mine doesn't work yet, from what I think is a fairly common problem. Let's fix it and do a demo. Vintage curve tracers are a load of fun for exploring basic electronics, and very useful for vintage work. The Tek 577, and its predecessor the 576, are, for good reason, much thought after curve tracer classics.

videos.t: Summer Interns vs. Friden H8 Mechanical Calculator
videos.desc:
The Computer History Museum Summer Interns take on the Friden H8 Mechanical Calculator from 1941. Interns win ;-) .
Tim Robinson (who just got the best of show award at the VCF West festival here: https://youtu.be/2bbsgfanbE0 ) has kindly donated a Friden H8 calculator to the Museum. It is entirely jammed - nothing moves. The Museum brilliant idea is to turn our summer interns loose on it! Well, not really that loose, I'll watch over closely... We could not find any documentation on the web about this early machine, and we have very limited time. So we'll discover as we go. Success not guarant

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 5 - hooking up the logic analyzer
videos.desc:
Last time we confirmed that the processor was running microcode and switching tasks. It's time to hook up the logic analyzer and look into more details into what's happening during the boot sequence. Ken Shirriff's detailed blog post about this session can be found here:
http://www.righto.com/2016/09/xerox-alto-restoration-day-5-smoke-and.html

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 6 - debug leads us to a failed IC
videos.desc:
Last time we were successful in recording our first Logic Analyzer traces of the boot process. Today, analyzer traces leads to missing disc task leads to bad card leads to bad IC leads to IC repair hack. Still no boot, but the Alto gets much further along in the process.
As usual, for more technical details, Ken Shirriff's in-depth blog entry about this session:
http://www.righto.com/2016/09/restoring-ycombinators-xerox-alto-day-6.html

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 7 - developing tools while waiting for new boot disk
videos.desc: This is an interim session as we await (anxiously) a known-good boot disc for the Alto. Most of the work happened off camera and off session. Ken was able to decipher most of the very long Logic Analyzer trace we obtained in session 6. He concluded that the entire boot sector of the disc is now read correctly, with no errors. But our disk is not a boot disc. It just has random data on it. And not just any kind of random data: Ken was able to trace it to a particular disc drive test program that used to be run on Altos to verify Diablo discs (read the details of his fascinating techno-detective

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 8 - Alto finally boots
videos.desc: We think we are pretty close to having our Xerox Alto boot. At the last session, the Logic Analyzer trace of the microcode boot process looked OK. However we determined that our disc had been erased with random data, many years ago probably, by a test program. The great folks at the Living Computer Museum came to our rescue and just sent us a boot disc platter with diagnostic programs on it. We are eager to test it and see if the Alto boots.

videos.t: HP 7970E Tape Drive Repair
videos.desc: My beloved monster HP 7970E vintage 9-track tape drive is not working anymore! It was fine working continuously during the two days of the VCF exhibition, but when I brought it home it would not load tape anymore. Time to look at the innards and find what is wrong.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 9 - debug session leads us closer to crashes root cause
videos.desc: Now that the Alto finally boots, we investigate why some programs, including the all important MADTEST hardware diagnostic, crash. This leads us to another wild hardware bug chase in the control RAM logic. For detailed technical background, see Ken's blog posting here: http://www.righto.com/2016/10/restoring-ycs-xerox-alto-day-9-tracing.html

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 10 - solving the crashes, first look at the GUI
videos.desc:
We solve the crashing problem, which was due to a Control ROM / CRAM board mismatch. Which allows us to finally run the diagnostic test suite. Which gives us a clean bill of  heath! If we only had a mouse that worked, we could use the Alto! PARC, whose support has been unwavering, lends us an original mouse on the spot later that day, and I get to try the famed GUI for the first time.
As usual, more technical details in Ken's blog entry:
http://www.righto.com/2016/10/restoring-ycs-xerox-alto-day-10-new.html

videos.t: LED Light Bulb Failure
videos.desc: My experience with LED lighting has been dismal. This promising technology is a little wet behind the ears. Although they are advertised to last for a very long time, justifying their much higher price, a large number of the bulbs I bought failed in a few month - way earlier than a much cheaper regular light bulb. Why is it? LEDs in themselves should be way more reliable than incandescent light bulbs. We take one apart to find out. This is an Ecosmart branded "75W" replacement bulb from Home Depot (manufactured by  Lighting Science Group Corporation). Says on the package: "lasts 25x longer tha

videos.t: Ted Kennedy’s 1969 Massachusetts driver license replica made on my IBM keypunch for a movie
videos.desc:
I was contacted by a movie production to make some props for an upcoming movie about the Chappaquiddick incident, namely a reproduction of Ted Kennedy’s driving license. Like the original,  I will make it on my restored 1960s IBM punched card machine and my IBM Selectric typewriter.

This is in 1969 when Ted Kennedy drove off a bridge, tragically resulting in the drowning of a young female campaign staffer and ensuing scandal. They needed replicas of 1960's Massachusetts driving licenses and applications, which were done on punched cards. They sent me photos of original licenses that I had to

videos.t: Richard Thomson's vintage computer collection
videos.desc: Richard Thomson gave me a tour of his collection while I was on business travel in Salt Lake City. He has quite an impressive collection centered on Computer Graphics, which is his trade. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

videos.t: Tektronix Oscilloscope Music
videos.desc:
I recently picked up a vintage Tektronix 603 X-Y monitor. Time to draw nice pictures with sound to showcase it! And when the Tek is paired with music from talented Austria-based artist (not Dutch as I mistakenly say in the video) Jerobeam Fenderson, it becomes truly spectacular. 
Music files can be obtained from: 
http://oscilloscopemusic.com/
The track played in the video at 8:53 is "Shrooms".

Here are some videos of Hansi and Jerobeam (Chris) showing some of the behind the scenes "making of": 
This great talk by Hansi about the software development and how he met Chris: 
https://youtu.be/iM

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 11 - exploring Draw and Bravo
videos.desc: Xerox corporate archives sent us a second mechanical mouse, and after careful cleaning it works really well. This allows us to take a deeper look at "Bravo" (the text editor) and "Draw" (the drawing program). We thank Xerox once again for their support of this project.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 12 - Ethernet pioneers and the first optical mouse
videos.desc: This video is dedicated to the fond memory of Ron Crane, who left us on June 19, 2017. We bring up the Ethernet card and optical mouse, and are visited by Xerox Ethernet inventors and pioneer designers Dave Boggs and Ron Crane. [ Edit: and David Boggs left us on Feb. 19, 2022, leaving behind a world that runs on Ethernet.]

videos.t: Vintage Tech Photoshoot with Kevin Twomey
videos.desc:
Showing their amazing old-tech innards in front of the camera:
- HP 7970E 9-track tape drive (1974)
- Solari Dator 10 mechanical flip clock (1957)
- HP 8662A 1.3 GHz signal generator (1981)
- Friden STW-10 mechanical calculator (1956)
- Friden EC-130 first transistorized calculator (1961)
- IBM Executary 214 magnetic band recorder (1964)

videos.t: New Year Flip on the Solari Dator 10 Flip Clock
videos.desc: The Italian-made 1957 Solari Dator 10 clock does its best move: the New Year Flip. And wishes you a happy nerdy new year.

videos.t: HP 6060B Electronic Load
videos.desc: I recently picked up an HP 6060B electronic load at an auction, along with a HP 6645A lab power supply and a vintage 3455A DVM to add to my collection of vintage HP instruments. These will be  used in a power supply test rig, for other restorations. Sure enough, the 6060B did not work. Oh, well, yet another awesome piece of vintage HP gear to repair.

videos.t: IBM System/360 Front Panel
videos.desc: I recently acquired this front panel from an IBM 360 mod 50, with lots of switches and over 250 blinkenlights. The IBM System/360 was an iconic mainframe computer introduced in 1964 (see promotional video here: https://youtu.be/V4kyTg9Cw8g). The system was a huge development gamble for IBM, with all the "models" from small to huge sharing mostly the same overall architecture and instruction set, but with radically different hardware implementations depending on the cost and performance point. A key novelty was the introduction of "SLT" ceramic hybrid modules, pre-dating the integrated circuit,

videos.t: Refilling or Replacing Vintage HP Plotter Pens
videos.desc: If you own a vintage HP plotter, you have certainly been faced with the vexing problem of finding new pens without paying a ransom to some ebay seller of dried out pens. Here is how I revive mine, by refilling or making adapter holders for entirely new pens.

videos.t: Alto Restoration Part 13  - Tools Development Struggle
videos.desc: These last few session have led to slow progress as we go through the arduous task of developing and debugging our own tools: an FPGA based disc tool that simulates the Alto writing and reading from disc, and a BeagleBone based Ethernet tool that simulates a pre-standard 3 MB Ethernet network that the Alto can connect to.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 14 - playing Astroroids
videos.desc: Xerox PARC graciously loaned us a couple historical Alto disc platters. We setup to explore their contents, and find as usual pretty surprising stuff for a 1970's machine (Ethernet phone anyone?). We end up trying a few games.

videos.t: IBM 3420 9-track tape drives arrrive for restoration. 800 lbs each!
videos.desc: I might have fallen into the deep end. It started with the IBM 360 control panel (https://youtu.be/WS-WtjwAAO0). Now I am adding some  rather heavy bits to complete the system.

videos.t: Candle Powered Thermoelectric-inator
videos.desc: I had been planning to play with my reclaimed thermoelectric cooler for a long time. I got inspired by this video: https://youtu.be/6LmDAFBBPK8. Let's explore how these fascinating miniature solid state heat pumps work.

videos.t: IBM 1401 Restoration Team: A Day at the Office
videos.desc: I put together a shorter video (warning: no new material here, this is cut from two previously released videos!) for an upcoming museum conference, to convey the behind-the-scenes restoration work on our 1959 IBM 1401 mainframe compusaur. There is some editing license as this uses takes from several debugging sessions, but I think it captures our team's joys and struggles pretty well. See the complete debugging session videos from which this was cut: https://youtu.be/7Lh4CMz_Z6M and https://youtu.be/PwftXqJu8hs.

videos.t: PDP-1 Demo at the CHM (short version)
videos.desc:
The "reader's digest" version of the full length PDP-1 video I just posted. WARNING: No New Material! Just a much shorter 2 min executive summary, targeted for a conference presentation at the end of the month. Watch the full length video here: https://youtu.be/1EWQYAfuMYw. 
This machine is on display at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California: http://www.computerhistory.org/

videos.t: Lyle Bickley explains the PDP-1 (and we play the original Spacewar!)
videos.desc: Lyle Bickley, of the PDP-1 restoration team, gives us a tour of this amazing, early scientific interactive computer at the Computer History Museum. The first machine built by DEC in 1959, it features a superb graphics screen. DEC gave one to MIT, and some very bright students went wild. Gems such as Spacewar!, Snowflake, 4-voice music programs were all developed by moonlighting MIT students, unencumbered by its measly 12kW memory and pokey 100,000 instructions per second. Along with much more serious debugging and programming languages of course. You can come and see the real machine for yours

videos.t: R2-D2 at Maker Faire Bay Area 2017
videos.desc: After a last minute repair, R2 spends a day at the Maker Faire Bay Area 2107. And I meet Rinoa Super-Genius! Rinoa actually made a better video than mine: https://youtu.be/7cX9vbKwSB8 .

videos.t: Inside the dome: R2-D2 emergency  repair
videos.desc: R2-D2 took a spill during Maker Faire's first day. An emergency repair is needed, which is a good opportunity to see what's inside the dome.

videos.t: Working on my R2-D2 Skins
videos.desc:
R2-D2 needs his skins, so he can look better for Maker Faire. This detailed building video is intended as an illustration to my build log on astromech.net. You'll find all the gory details here:
http://astromech.net/forums/showthread.php?2957-CuriousMarc-R2-D2-Build-Log

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 15 - Ethernet mysteries solved, Alto back in one piece
videos.desc:
This video is dedicated to the memory of Chuck Thacker (February 26, 1943 – June 12, 2017), primary architect of the Alto hardware. 
The last Ethernet hardware mysteries are solved and we are able to do some primitive exchanges with the Alto over the network. Which means we are done with the main hardware restoration! It's time to take the Alto off life support and put it back together. After one big scare, our restored Alto is back in his cabinet, looking spiffy, and ready for demos and exhibitions.

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 16 - our disk goes down, the Alto connects to Google and draws fractals
videos.desc: Our Diablo disk goes on the fritz, but who needs a disk when you can netboot? Ken demonstrates the Alto network capabilities, connects to Google, and has the Alto calculate and display a Mandlebrot set. Ken's in-depth blog entry including the fractal demo source code is found here: http://www.righto.com/2017/06/one-hour-mandelbrot-creating-fractal-on.html

videos.t: Droid Transport
videos.desc: For illustrating my Curious Marc R2-D2 build log on Astromech.net. My cart for transporting R2-D2. Video was released a long time ago but for some reason was unlisted and could only be accessed through Astromech.net. Just changed it to public which makes it look much newer that it is. This is back from October 2011, when it had no dome panels, no holoprojectors, and legs were unfinished.

videos.t: Panasonic Toughbook CF-U1, Jedi's best friend?
videos.desc: I finally met Rinoa Super Genius in the real world, and she even had a very nice gift for me: a somewhat sticky 2008 Panasonic Toughbook CF-U1, fresh from her favorite surplus place. I happen to love small all-in-one portable units, so let's see how this cute rugged one fares. Check out Rinoa's channel here: https://www.youtube.com/user/icc3a1800

videos.t: Xerox Alto Restoration Part 17 - Xerox Alto Demo
videos.desc: We take you through a demo of our restored Xerox Alto. We go through the Neptune file browser, the Bravo text editor, the Draw and SIL programs, network booting, ftp, telnet, Smalltalk, some games and new programs we have made for the Alto. This demo was developed to be presented live at VCF West 2017. And I mispelled Ken's last name, it's Ken Shirriff.

videos.t: Vintage Computer Festival 2017: Xerox Alto meets its inventors, wins a price and other highlights
videos.desc: From my video snippets of the 2017 Vintage Computer Festival West which we just participated in. We had our Alto (proudly) on display. I had enough time to interview some of my favorite exhibitors. It is not exhaustive, so not much post 1970's stuff or micro's, of which there was plenty... But it should give you a good flavor of what the show is about. Come see us next time!

videos.t: CuriousMarc's Eclipse 2017 Adventure
videos.desc: Finally, an eclipse I can view with my larger telescope! I defy traffic jams, volcanoes, overzealous police, dead camera batteries, and menacing clouds to successfully see the 2017 total eclipse in Oregon. And even make friends with cheerful local native Americans. Many thanks to my friend and colleague Eric Zbinden for his awesome astrophotos of the eclipse, and to Robert Garner for the totality picture in Madras.

videos.t: Bob Rosenbloom's Vintage Computer Collection
videos.desc:
Bob Rosenbloom is one of the prominent collectors of vintage computers in our area. His impressive collection is tucked away in hangars and containers on his remote property, surrounded by giant Redwood trees. Always a treat to pay him a visit. 

More details on his website here: http://www.dvq.com

videos.t: My first computer: the 1976 SC/MP 8-Bit Microprocessor Kit
videos.desc: Although the SC/MP is very special to me, it must have been one of the most under-powered 8-bit microprocessors unleashed at the time (1976). But I didn't know any better, and in my 14-year old eyes, it was nothing short of amazing. This was my first computer hands-on experience. I discovered microprocessor fundamentals and assembly programming with it, all in the glory of raw hexadecimal machine coding. I found my beloved kit again during a visit at my parents, along with my notes, and brought it back to its native Silicon Valley birthplace (the National Semi plant, now Texas Instruments, is

videos.t: R2LA 2017: Star Wars robot builders meeting
videos.desc:
R2LA is the largest annual gathering of the R2 (and other Star Wars robots) builders club. It's equal parts wacky Star Wars fandom, impressive robot engineering, and film prop artistry. We gathered no less than 42 full size R2-D2 replicas, plus a load of other BB-8's and Mouse Droids, many quite amazing.

Our sponsor for PCBs: https://www.pcbway.com
Support the team on Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/curiousmarc
Merch on Teespring: https://teespring.com/stores/curiousmarcs-store
Learn more on companion site: https://www.curiousmarc.com
Contact info: https://www.youtube.com/curiousmarc/about

videos.t: My 1957 Friden Mechanical Calculator goes on Japanese TV
videos.desc:
My 1957 Friden STW 10 mechanical calculator is due for an appearance in a high quality documentary about women that made mathematical calculations for NASA. But before the filming, I need to make sure it works.

Friden Calculator Playlist: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5_GbzkFwdKpuyPo8Ty83h8b

More about the Friden STW10 on my website:
https://www.curiousmarc.com/mechanical/friden-stw-10-mechnical-calculator

Our sponsor for PCBs: https://www.pcbway.com
Support the team on Patreon: https://www.patreon.com/curiousmarc
Buy shirts on Teespring: https://teespring.com/stores/curiousm

videos.t: IBM Vintage Mainframe Peripherals Hauling Expedition
videos.desc: I just bought a vintage 1200 lines per minute IBM mainframe line printer on fleabay! It weighs in at 400 lbs, so it's local pickup only. Time to take a truck, visit the place and see what other treasures we can find.

videos.t: Digibarn Alto Part 1: Another Xerox Alto arrives for restoration
videos.desc:
Our second Xerox Alto arrives from the Digibarn, courtesy of Dr. Bruce Damer. Bruce also brought a chord keyset that we were missing on our first Alto. Unfortunately the Digibarn Alto seems to be made out of reject parts and was inhabited by little critters. This will be challenging...
Link to the Digibarn: http://www.digibarn.com/

videos.t: Digibarn Alto Part 2: Restoring the Power Supplies from Hell
videos.desc: All of the switching power supplies from our Xerox Alto from the Digibarn are bad. All of them! And the main LH Research Mighty Mite 5V/60A power supply is putting up a real fight. By the time I start this video, we are a good week into troubleshooting it, with a growing pile of bad parts and no end in sight.

videos.t: Digibarn Alto Part 3: Restoring the CRT Monitor
videos.desc: The rat-infested Digibarn monitor isn't even meant to be connected to an Alto, and does not work either. But we find a way to retrofit it to the Alto, and find that a tiny light bulb buried in the high voltage circuitry is the cause of the failure. More details about what a bulb is doing in the circuit on Ken's blog (and don't believe the inane comments, it is not used a fuse): http://www.righto.com/2017/10/inside-vintage-xerox-altos-display-tiny.html

videos.t: Digibarn Alto Part 4: Will it boot?
videos.desc:
We put the Digibarn Alto back together. Difficultly, because it's missing bits and pieces. Will it boot?
June 2021 Update: Restoration has now been completed, see here: https://youtu.be/Qh-4kNWbpMc

videos.t: Macintosh 512K Part 1: Unboxing and Restoration
videos.desc: Taking a break from complicated Alto repairs, we take care of its heir, the Apple Macintosh. This 512Ke (e for "extended") came packed in its original box, so we can do an unboxing! Easy peasy "restoration" as only the floppy drive does not work, but that's a good excuse to open it up. The HD20 hard drive, on the other hand, is a more challenging repair in this other video: https://youtu.be/r2RkTCkUNaY

videos.t: The IBM 1401 Mainframe Computer Wishes you a Merry Christmas
videos.desc: Ken Shirriff uses the computing power of our vintage 1959 IBM mainframe at the Computer History Museum for holiday mischief. More info on Ken's blog at: http://www.righto.com/2017/12/creating-christmas-card-on-vintage-ibm_7.html

videos.t: Macintosh 512K Part 2: HD20 Hard Drive Restoration
videos.desc: The Mac 512Ke works, but the external HD20 20 MB disc does not even spin up. We'll try to repair it, leading to open-disk surgery.

videos.t: Beats Pill 2.0 Battery Replacement (Beats Pill won't turn on or charge)
videos.desc: My repair of a recent Beats Pill 2.0 that did not want to charge anymore. Apparently many, many people have that problem. Turns out it's one of the battery cells that's dead. Warning: features unremarkable consumer hardware that does not work. Vintage fans of my other superbly-engineered, milestone-setting hardware, move right along.

videos.t: Vintage HP Mini Cartridge Tapes Part 2: Tape Salad (Refurbishing DC100 and DC2000 Tapes)
videos.desc:
This shows how to refurbish one of the pesky DC100 or DC2000 mini-cartridge tapes. They fail in a million different ways, all leading to a particular recipe of tape salad. But (with quite a bit of effort), you can beat them in submission to work reliably again.
The bands used to repair the tapes are 4-¼ inch Plastibands.

See Part 1: https://youtu.be/cTZCD4OXETk

videos.t: Vintage HP Mini Cartridge Tapes Part 1: Refurbishing  Drives (HP 85, HP 9825, HP 2645)
videos.desc:
The HP mini-cartridge tapes are the bane of vintage HP collectors: they are necessary to  make the equipment work, but pretty much guaranteed to have failed by now. I show how to refurbish the 3 slightly different mechanisms (HP 85, HP 9825 and HP 2645): how to scrape and re-coat the capstan, extend its length for DC2000 use, and make the necessary write current adjustment for the DC2000 and modern Athana recreations of the DC100 tapes.  In Part 2 we will repair the tape cartridges themselves.

The rubber used for the repair is called Plasti Dip.

videos.t: Powering a 1955 IBM 705 Vacuum Tube Logic Module
videos.desc:
We like to see things glow on Christmas. Why not old computer circuits? Carl has an IBM 705 module in his collection, with 8 vacuum tubes. It dates back from about 1955, and is an impressive retro-tech piece. But Master Ken wants to see how it actually works. He somehow managed to reverse engineer Carl's module (I'll link to his blog article once it's up). He just brought it to the lab, where I barely have enough high-voltage equipment to power it up. What does it do? Will it still work after 50 years? 

Link to Ken's articles, Part I: http://www.righto.com/2018/01/examining-1954-ibm-mainframe

videos.t: HP 2645 Terminal - Part 1: Overview and Adding New Fonts
videos.desc: This is a multi-part series for HP and terminal lovers, focusing on the HP 264x terminal series from 1974-1982. We start with the HP 2645A, which is said to be the most common, although these are quite rare and pricey nowadays. The original HP 264x were  expensive ($5000 in 1975 for a base HP 2645A), professional grade terminals engineered for reliability and productivity. No expense was spared on the inductive pickup keyboard, the wide aspect ratio screen, and the integrated mini-cartridge tapes. And the bipolar 9-bit character ROMs chips, a rare beast indeed. The series was originally powere

videos.t: HP 2645 Terminal - Part 2: Large Character Set Upgrade and Terminal Demo
videos.desc:
This is a multi-part series for HP and terminal lovers, focusing on the HP 264x terminal series from 1974-1982. DEMO STARTS AT 14:30 . After the 8-bit alphanumeric Math character set upgrade from the previous video, we attempt the more involved 9-bit microvector Large Character set upgrade. Which temporarily screws up the previous hack. When we recover, we can finally use the full capabilities of the terminal. The newly gained table drawing and forms editing capability are more impressive than I suspected, and I have not hooked it up to a computer yet!
Documents, font maps and ROM dumps at htt

videos.t: Alto Restoration Part 18 - We crash our disk drive. Mill to the rescue!
videos.desc: While archiving the original Xerox PARC cartridges, we occasionally crash our drives heads. Usually, these are minor crashes, caused by disk defects (previous crashes mostly) or simply by picking up some old flaking magnetic oxide on the heads. Just cleaning the heads and the disk will allow to recover. But at the last session, both our main and backup drives crashed hard on particularly difficult media. We don't dare putting any other disk in them until we to take the heads out for inspection, repair or replacement. Which means we have to do a dreaded drive realignment afterwards. Fortunately

videos.t: The IBM 1401 compiles and runs FORTRAN II
videos.desc:
We attempt to compile and run a simple FORTRAN program on our vintage 1959 IBM mainframe computer at the Computer History Museum. FORTRAN is a big stretch for this business oriented machine, with 16k memory and a CPU not meant at all for  scientific applications. Even integer multiply and divide instructions are  an optional feature on the base machine!  Success not guaranteed.

Come see the IBM 1401 computer at the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California, USA:
https://computerhistory.org/exhibits/ibm1401/

Simulation and programming environment available here: https://github.com/

videos.t: HP 2645 Terminal - Part 3: Living the ASCII Life
videos.desc:
This is a multi-part series for HP and terminal lovers, focusing on the HP 264x terminal series from 1974-1982. Now that we have loaded fancy fonts, it's time to connect it to a computer. And live the 1970 life in full black and white ASCII.
Documents, font maps and ROM dumps at https://www.curiousmarc.com/computing/hp-264x-terminals

videos.t: HP 2645 Terminal - Part 4: The First 8-Bit Gaming Console?
videos.desc:
This is a multi-part series for HP and terminal lovers, focusing on the HP 264x terminal series from 1974-1982. In this episode, we manage to load and play (really good!) games on this 8-bit terminal from 1975. Would that make it the first 8-bit personal gaming station?
Documents, font maps and ROM dumps at:
