videos.t: CuriousMarc is on Gizmodo!
videos.desc:
Much better! Now right here on your tube: 
https://youtu.be/tJ2-kkhghD4
Come back here afterwards to post your likes and comments! 

The talented Gizmodo video crew came to my basement to make a short piece about me for their new "Show Me Your Nerd" series. Perfect for me, I have a lot of nerd to show. That was 10 hours of filming for 5 minutes of video, but it shows in the result!

videos.t: Tribute to Weird Stuff (and a partial collection tour)
videos.desc:
Weird Stuff, one of Silicon Valley's favorite surplus electronic store, is no more. That's a big loss for our local electro-nerdy community. As an homage to them, here is a partial tour of my collection, pointing out all the essential (weird) stuff they had contributed to my restorations. 
Music: After the Rain (Duke Pearson) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3qN-QTuMzL8

videos.t: Working for Friends: Sperry Univac UTS-40 and Haunted Diablo Drive
videos.desc: Today we are helping out friends for what we thought would be quick and easy projects. But they turned out to be quite difficult. I bought a Sperry Univac UTS-40 terminal for Dominique in Belgium, who needed the parts, and want to try to turn it on before I ship it. We also are helping Alto owner Michele from the East Coast, who sent us her Diablo disk drive that seems to crash anything you put in it.

videos.t: Michele's Haunted Diablo Drive
videos.desc: Michele is an Alto owner that sent us her malfunctioning Diablo disk drive. But Michele's Diablo drive seems haunted, cursed, and possessed - in one word, "diablolical". It destroys disks, heads, alignment cartridges and other drives sitting nearby. It even makes my lights flicker while we test it. And for the life of us, after we change all the parts, the ghosts are still in. But we won't give up until we exorcise it.

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 1: Volker's beautiful machine goes bad...
videos.desc: The 1990's Dolch Pac's are my favorite retro-PCs for lab support. They are portable, yet you can stick many old PCI and ISA interface cards in them. The Pac 65 Pentium II based computers are old enough to run DOS and Windows 98, but modern enough to run XP and Linux. However things go very wrong when I demonstrate how to setup this fine example...

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 2: reviving the motherboard from the dead
videos.desc: The motherboard of my venerable Dolch Pac 65 died during the filming of Episode I: The Dolch Menace. It's beeping in a two-tone siren. I don't have the schematics, so unless it's obvious, it's going to feel like poking in the dark.

videos.t: HP 1607A Logic Analyzer
videos.desc: We explore the 1975 HP 1607 Logic State Analyzer, one of the first logic analyzers, while noisy construction is going on in the background. And we conduct a completely impartial test on how it stacks up with a modern reincarnation.

videos.t: The IBM 1401 mainframe runs "Edith"
videos.desc:
This politically incorrect one is going to lose me the precious few female followers left on my channel. But for the good of academic research, we were asked to run the program "Edith" on the vintage 1959 IBM mainframe at the computer history museum. Which goes on to prove that the more technology evolves, the more things stay the same. And I forgot how to pronounce the alphabet in German.
Original  code and IBM 1401 emulator to run it can be found on my website:
https://www.curiousmarc.com/computing/ibm-1401-mainframe/ibm-1401-edith

Our sponsor for PCBs: https://www.pcbway.com
Support the te

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 3: the MiniPro TL866A programmer fixes a BIOS chip
videos.desc:
We found out that the culprit for my dead Dolch PAC65 was a bad BIOS chip during the filming of Episode II: The Dolch Strikes Back. Thanks to EBay and cheapie but goodie Chinese EPROM programmers, we should be able to reflash the BIOS and find out what was wrong with it in the first place. Will the venerable Dolch be resurrected? 

BIOS images uploaded here: https://www.curiousmarc.com/computing/dolchpac-65

Sorry for the awful Youtube generated blurring, I did not realize the addresses were legible and didn't want to re-upload the video...

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 4: Windows 98 Installation
videos.desc: We relive a full Windows 98 install on our now working Dolch PAC 65 hardware. My, is it painful. How did we ever suffer through it. Sorry, nothing breaks in this video, except for me installing right on top of my NT partition while I am proudly trying to show how to avoid it...

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 5: How to setup file sharing between Windows 98 and Windows 7
videos.desc: I show how to network Win98 and Win7 so you can use the native Windows file sharing. This is a public service technical "how-to" video for the few crackpots that want to run Win98 and are faced with this odd problem. And for me to remember how I did it.

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 6: Adding Soundblaster, SCSI,  GPIB and USB cards to a Win98 computer
videos.desc: Our Dolch PAC 65 is repaired and running Win98! We add a Soundblaster Live! Card, a PCI USB2 card, an old Adaptec SCSI and ISA National Instruments GPIB card to make it a capable retro-tool. Quite a bit of work to make all that function correctly under Win98 and DOS, as you will see in the video.

videos.t: Dolch Pac 65 - Part 7:  Windows XP and Crunchbang Linux installation, and quintuple boot!
videos.desc: Finally, we add WinXP and Linux to the mix, and then try to quintuple boot it (DOS/Win98/WinNT/WinXP/Linux). For Linux I use the lightweight but mighty CrunchBang distro. Some secret maneuver needed for XP and the usual Linux command line Kung-Fu required.

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 - Part 1: A Teletype Arrives for Restoration
videos.desc:
A Teletype recently arrived for restoration. It's an early one, a Model 19, which actually incorporates a Model 15 keyboard and printer unit first introduced in 1930. This Model 19 was a military version made for the Army Signal Corps, and was a mainstay in WWII. The gray paint on ours indicates it was likely deployed in the Navy. It uses 5-bit serial Baudot code for communication, a predecessor of the 8-bit ASCII code that later Teletypes would use. We inspect the unit for the first time after an initial rough cleaning.

Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 2: Baudot Teletype Intro and Demo
videos.desc:
We show our partially restored Model 15 to explain the basics of 5-bit Baudot teletypes. In addition to showing off this incredible machine, it should provide a good background to better follow the upcoming Model 19 restoration.


Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5-9eQLTCk9xx16RAGEYHH1q

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 3: Teardown time!
videos.desc:
We are starting the restoration work on the  1930's model 19 Teletype, and two other model 15s while we are at it. Some of the model 19 assemblies are stripped entirely bare for repainting. In the process we discover new things about the innards of our machines.

Teletype Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5-9eQLTCk9xx16RAGEYHH1q

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 4: Thyratron Power Supply
videos.desc:
We attempt to turn on the REC-30 high voltage power supply. They call it a rectifier actually, not a power supply. It's supposed to deliver up to 0.6A at 200V. The monstrous vintage 1930 design uses beautiful giant Thyratron tubes . Will it glow or will it blow?
See Ken Shirriff's in-depth article about the inner workings of this supply: http://www.righto.com/2018/09/glowing-mercury-thyratrons-inside-1940s.html

videos.t: Why we don't always replace vintage electrolytic capacitors
videos.desc:
Judging from the comments on my last video, there is much misconception about if and when to replace vintage electrolytic capacitors. This video explain why, contrary to widespread internet lore, we don't feel compelled to replace all of our vintage electrolytic caps. Caveat emptor: although we are engineers in real life, we are dabbling hobbyists when it comes to component reliability. The physics and statistics of reliability is very heady stuff better left to specialized scientists and requires very complicated investigations.

Teletype Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 5: We make vintage baudot bits!
videos.desc: In this episode, we restore our Model 19 Teletype keyboard and tape punch, and generate our first 1930-vintage Baudot bits!

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 6: Fixing the keyboard counter, filter and repeat features
videos.desc:
We continue our Model 19 Teletype keyboard and punch work with the restoration with some intriguing features, none of them working of course...

Teletype Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5-9eQLTCk9xx16RAGEYHH1q

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 7: Our First Intergalactic Transmission Attempt
videos.desc:
While waiting for the model 19 to take a bath, we attempt for the first time to transmit from one model 15 to the other. They are separated by at least 10 feet. Which in my book is a distance of intergalactic proportion. Will it print?

Teletype Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5-9eQLTCk9xx16RAGEYHH1q

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 8: Printer Restoration (and a Teletype-quarium)
videos.desc:
Time to restore the most complex mechanical assembly of our Model 19 teletype: the receiver/printer. Which momentarily finds itself the center piece of a newly invented Teletype-quarium.

Teletype Model 19 Restoration Playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL-_93BVApb5-9eQLTCk9xx16RAGEYHH1q

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 9: Fixing the Model 15
videos.desc:
My hand-me-down Model 15 is behaving oddly. Turns out most of it is hard to diagnose, self-inflicted damage from previous restoration efforts. Fear not, it all ends well. But a long video is needed to tell the woes. However, we repair and discover all kind of new things: the motor stop feature, the unshift on blank, and the mute on blank. Clever machines they are.
 Useful links to stuff seen in the video:
- "Jedi" Panasonic Toughbook restoration: https://youtu.be/mQHGFHK-ldA
- John Nagle's baudotrss software: 
http://www.aetherltd.com/communicating.html
- John Nagle's ttyloopinterface 60 mA in

videos.t: Teletype Model 19 Part 10: Restoring the Transmitter/Distributor
videos.desc:
We got a fair bit of our Teletype machines running now: we can send from the keyboard, receive and print, and can punch 5-bit baudot paper tapes. But we can not read and send our punch tapes yet. videos.t: Core Memory Explained and Demonstrated
videos.desc:
Ferrite core memory was the dominant computer memory technology from the 1950s to the late 1970s. Before we delve into the repair of our Apollo AGC core memory, I thought it would be good to explain how they work, as they are very different from modern semiconductor memory. 

Check out our Russian core memory follow up video here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7ozNMgx7WtQ

Ken Shirriff has some of the best core memory write ups I know of, here:
http://www.righto.com/2015/08/examining-core-memory-module-inside.html
This one details the AGC core memory:
http://www.righto.com/2019/01/inside-apo

Much better versions of this gyro were used in the Apollo Inertial Measurement Unit used by the guidance computer. But similar principles apply. We eventually plan to use original Apollo servo electronics with this or a similar gyroscope.

Visit Ed Thelen's (who brought us the gyros for this episode) page on gyroscopes: http://ed-thelen.org/Gyroscope.html

Our AGC actually did not come with flight rope modules, but instead with a pair of Raytheon boxes used during development for simulating the final ropes. videos.t: Teletype 33 ASR Part 1: Restoration Begins
videos.desc:
We jump ahead a giant 30 years from the previous Teletype model we restored, and gain 3 bits in the process. Our Teletype Model 33 ASR is an 8-bit ASCII device, introduced in 1963,  compatible with the brand spanking new ASCII standard. Actually, calling it 8-bit is pushing it, as it transmits only 7-bit ASCII characters. The 8th bit is for an optional parity. But the new machine is a screamer, running at the blazing speed of 110 bauds (compared to our 1930's Model 15 that ran at 45.5 bauds).

videos.t: We Rediscover Spark Gap Radio by Accident
videos.desc:
It's 1890 all over again in the lab. By complete accident, I find myself the new owner of a high voltage box that turns out to be a vintage Xenon lamp sparker. Not only do we make it work, but we use it to retrace the critical experiments that led to the discovery of radio, using the lamp starter as the spark gap transmitter, and a coherer as the receiver. 

Ken’s blog article gives more details about the reverse engineering of the Siemens sparker:

[2024 edit] This video is dedicated to the fond memory of Ed Thelen. Ed left us peacefully on Sept. 14, 2024, having kept his contagious laugh, humor, and insatiable curiosity for engineering until the ripe age of 93. videos.t: HP 5245L Nixie Counter - Part 1: The King of 1960s Frequency Meters
videos.desc:
We start repairing our very broken HP 5245L. It is arguably the king of the Nixie frequency meters of the 1960s. Equipped with the right plug in, it could count up to 18 GHz. It feels like repairing a giant IC, but with access to every transistor. We're sure not complaining about it.

videos.t: Apollo 13 accident: understanding Houston’s real time debug (Apollo Comms Part 28)
videos.desc:

Using the original schematics, looking how our inverter was hooked up in the power system, we can follow word for word the Apollo 13 raw audio of the debug after the accident. I will go into much more engineering details than what is usually reported, but once you understand this, the flight control loops become both limpid and downright chilling. And then, when we regain our composure and get back to said inverter, more surprises await.

videos.t: Apollo Comms Part 30: We explain and debug modern (CD4046B) and vintage (Apollo) PLL circuits.
videos.desc:
We build a Phase Locked Loop (PLL) FM demodulator for extracting the Apollo downvoice from its subcarrier, using the classic 7046B IC. But in the meantime, as luck would have it, NASA's own S-band receiver's PLL seems to have gone bonkers, and we can't lock to the spacecraft microwave downlink anymore! So we'll get very hands on with PLLs in this episode. Expect a healthy dose of PLL elevator music.

videos.t: Modern Fails: Newall C80 DRO repair
videos.desc:

So, we reverse engineer it, and find out that the proprietary principle of operation is absolutely genius, involving ball bearings and magnetics, with a readout precision of better than 10 microns. And the fault is quite unexpected. Hint: not a capacitor. 

Update: Master Ken decapped the ferro-electric memory chip and made a blog about it, showing pictures of the unusual chip and explaining how it works. See it here: http://www.righto.com/2024/09/ramtron-ferroelectric-fram-die.html

videos.t: Titan missile in silo
videos.desc: Decommissioned Titan II nuclear missile in its silo. This is the largest nuclear missile ever made by the US during the cold war. 54 of these monsters were ready to be launched in less than a minute. Thanks goodness we never launched any, and they were decommissioned. Most ended up being used by NASA for launching satellites, and more importantly, the later Gemini missions. The silos were destroyed after the SALT agreement, and this is the only preserved one, at the Titan Missile Museum in Tucson, AZ.
